abstracts.value: Realistic simulation of quantum key distribution (QKD) networks requires a combination of precise models of quantum channels and network functions. Unfortunately, existing QKD network simulators lack either rigorous quantum physics modeling or network key-management and routing protocols, which limit their practical applicability. To address this limitation, we propose a QKD network simulator with hyperparameter tuning (QKDSim-HT), a NetSquid-based simulator specialized for polarization-based discrete-variable QKD networks. Specifically, QKDSim-HT models properties in quantum physics (photon loss, polarization-dependent depolarization, detector inefficiencies, dark counts, and dead times) as well as advanced functionalities in networking algorithms (multi-hop key relay and adaptive routing). Extensive simulations over diverse topologies reveal that the networking performance varied with respect to the fundamental properties of quantum physics, such as depolarization, fiber length, and channel attenuation. As a representative use case of QKDSim-HT, simulation results from QKDSim-HT over simple examples clearly manifest that a design of QKD networks highly affects performance of the networks. Accordingly, QKDSim-HT can serve as a practical platform for performance evaluation and optimization of quantum secured network.

titles.title: Quantum Key Distribution Network Simulator With Hyperparameter Tuning for Realistic Performance Analysis

abstracts.value: We have developed a synthetic fused-silica based Kaon Veto Cherenkov counter (KVC) for the J-PARC E72 experiment, which aims to explore hyperon resonances near the Λη threshold via K−p reactions. The KVC is required to reject beam-through kaons in the momentum range of 0.65–0.95 GeV/c, corresponding to the velocity region of β≈0.8–0.9, with high efficiency (>99%) under a 1.0 T magnetic field. A major technical challenge in this velocity region is that the Cherenkov angle is approximately 31°–40° for kaons, which falls below the critical angle for total internal reflection (TIR) at the silica–air interface (θcrit≈43.2°), leading to light loss through the radiator side faces. To overcome this limitation, we applied a ground-glass finish to the radiator side faces to induce diffuse scattering and redirect photons toward the sensor planes. In a beam test at the J-PARC K1.8BR beamline, the ground-glass configuration yielded a mean light yield of approximately 86Np.e., providing a factor-of-1.8 improvement over the 48Np.e. obtained with the conventional polished configuration. This enhancement provided a sufficient safety margin for stable operation. The detector was successfully operated throughout the J-PARC E72 physics run, achieving a detection efficiency of >99% and enabling stable data collection.

titles.title: Development of a quartz-based threshold Cherenkov Veto counter with MPPC Readout for a Hadron spectroscopy experiment at J-PARC

abstracts.value: Microchannel Plate Photomultiplier Tubes (MCP-PMT) devices represent the state-of-the-art in terms of picosecond timing resolution combined with low noise, high gain, and radiation hardness. However, with experiment upgrades producing higher luminosities, there are concerns over the ability of existing technologies to achieve sufficiently high rates and a longer tube lifetime in terms of extracted charge. To overcome these limitations, we are developing a hybrid diamond/MCP-PMT consisting of a transmission dynode followed by an MCP. The transmission dynode, a diamond-based composite material comprising a single crystal diamond membrane on a high open area support structure, operates at a gain of ∼10−20, followed by a further gain in the MCP. This high first gain stage produces a low gain variance which allows operation at a lower overall gain while maintaining the tight pulse height distribution (PHD) necessary for single photon counting. Since the maximum MCP signal is current-limited due to the MCP resistance, a lower overall gain allows a higher maximum photon count rate to be achieved. In addition, the diamond membrane acts as an impermeable barrier to ion feedback from the MCP, a major cause of photo-cathode degradation which limits the effective lifetime of conventional tubes. In the longer term, a complete replacement of MCPs with transmission dynodes is an attractive prospect. These devices would have an excellent single-photon spectrum, higher collection efficiency than MCP-PMTs and their linear geometry will give much improved timing precision over the ∼30 ps of conventional MCP-PMTs.

titles.title: Transmission dynodes: Enhancing vacuum photodetectors

abstracts.value: Gallium nitride (GaN) is one of the wide-bandgap semiconductor materials, which may have an excellent radiation tolerance beyond silicon and therefore be usable as a charged-particle sensor in future high-luminosity hadron colliders with severe radiation environment. Aiming for a GaN sensor capable of detecting a minimum-ionizing particle, we prototyped and characterized a GaN-based low-gain avalanche diode (LGAD). While no breakdown was observed up to 200 V, formation of the gain layer was confirmed from the capacitance and collected charge (measured using 5.48 MeV α particles from a 241Am source) as a function of the bias voltage. Moreover, basic radiation tolerance with an extreme radiation fluence was evaluated using a simple GaN pn-diode irradiated with 50 MeV protons up to 1.1×1016neq/cm2. These results provide fundamental insight into the detailed understanding of the GaN-LGAD and radiation tolerance of the GaN detectors.

titles.title: Characterization of gallium nitride-based particle detectors with p–n junction and low-gain avalanche diode structures

abstracts.value: Nuclear astrophysics experiments at low energies greatly benefit from the background reduction afforded by deep underground laboratories, allowing the detection of rare events from low-probability nuclear reactions. While the advantages of this approach are well-known for reactions emitting photons, this strategy has been exploited less for reactions emitting exclusively charged-particles. Here, we report on the construction and commissioning of a new charged-particle detection array designed for measurements of nuclear reactions at the LUNA-400 accelerator, located deep underground in INFN Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso (Italy). We describe the challenges and requirements for this array, and report on its performance for future physics studies.

titles.title: A new detection array for underground charged particle spectroscopy at LUNA-400

abstracts.value: Understanding the evolution of transverse beam profiles in high-intensity proton synchrotrons is crucial for stable, high-power operation. A residual gas ionization profile monitor (IPM) has been developed and commissioned for the Rapid Cycling Synchrotron (RCS) at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS) to enable non-invasive, bunch-by-bunch horizontal beam profile measurements. During commissioning, key challenges such as electromagnetic interference (EMI) from the high-intensity proton beam and accelerator components, insufficient microchannel plate (MCP) gain due to power supply limitations, and elevated vacuum pressure were addressed through RF shielding and an enhanced Faraday cage for EMI suppression, a pull-down resistor for optimal MCP gain, and an additional vacuum pump for pressure reduction. These improvements enabled successful commissioning, with a peak-finding algorithm and RF-synchronized window technique developed to identify individual bunches and reconstruct profiles. Measurements were performed in both ion and electron collection modes, revealing beam position and horizontal size distributions during the injection painting process. This paper details the IPM’s design, commissioning strategies, and data analysis methods for achieving bunch-by-bunch non-invasive beam profile observations.

titles.title: Fast residual gas ionization profile monitor for bunch-by-bunch beam profile measurements in the CSNS rapid cycling synchrotron

abstracts.value: We present a unified theoretical framework for analyzing both electrostatic two-stream and electromagnetic Weibel instabilities in counterstreaming electron-positron pair plasmas. Through systematic derivation of dispersion relations in non-relativistic and relativistic regimes, we demonstrate how the symmetric mass ratio fundamentally alters instability characteristics compared to electron-ion systems. The two-stream instability, driven by longitudinal electrostatic perturbations parallel to beam motion, exhibits enhanced growth rates in pair plasmas due to equal contributions from both species, with relativistic suppression scaling as γ0−3 for both electrons and positrons. The Weibel instability, arising from transverse electromagnetic modes perpendicular to streaming directions, lacks the heavy-ion stabilization present in electron-ion plasmas, producing broader unstable spectral ranges and modified saturation levels. We derive explicit conditions determining the relative dominance of each mechanism across parameter space defined by drift velocity, wavenumber orientation, and relativistic Lorentz factor. Our analysis shows that longitudinal two-stream modes dominate at small perpendicular wavenumbers and moderate drift velocities, while transverse Weibel modes become prevalent at high perpendicular wavenumbers and large velocity spreads or temperature anisotropies. These findings have direct implications for understanding magnetic field generation, particle acceleration, and energy dissipation in astrophysical pair plasmas including pulsar wind nebulae, gamma-ray burst internal shocks, and active galactic nuclei jets where counterstreaming pair populations naturally arise.

titles.title: Suppression of two-stream and Weibel instabilities in ultra-relativistic electron–positron plasma

abstracts.value: Realistic quantum devices are open systems, and their behaviour depends not only on the subsystem of interest but also on how the environment is modelled and how the relevant observables are extracted. This thesis studies that problem in three settings. First, we study cavity-assisted qubit readout beyond the dispersive regime. We show that once coherent excitation exchange and dissipation become relevant, a microscopic treatment is needed to describe the readout quantitatively, and the optimal readout is set by a trade-off between signal accumulation and the distinguishability of the readout states. Second, we compare fermionic and spin baths in non-interacting transport models and show that spin baths reproduce fermionic reduced dynamics only in the large-bath weak-coupling limit, while clear deviations appear for smaller baths and near half-filling. Third, we study charge transport in molecular junctions using Automated Compression of Environments (ACE). There, the main difficulty is not the time evolution itself, but the extraction of the transport current, since this observable depends on system-environment correlations and is therefore not contained in the reduced system density matrix alone. We show that a probe-mode construction provides a viable route to reformulate the current as a system observable. This thesis advances our understanding of what is required for accurate modelling of open quantum dynamics across a range of solid-state settings, from cavity-assisted qubit readout to charge transport in molecular junctions.

titles.title: Developing and validating models of open quantum systems in solid-state nanostructures

abstracts.value: The development of large-scale superconducting quantum computers critically depends on the accurate readout of qubit states. To enable this, cryogenic parametric amplifiers have been proposed and developed, and have since found widespread use in small-signal detection applications. Among various amplifier architectures, Josephson traveling-wave parametric amplifiers (JTWPAs) are widely adopted due to their broad bandwidth, high saturation power, and compatibility with superconducting qubits. In this work, we present a design workflow of JTWPAs based on a cosimulation approach combining electromagnetic (EM) and circuit-level simulation. We apply this method to a uniform JTWPA, comparing our simulation results with experimental data. To mitigate the challenge of constructing lumped-element circuit models usually used in the conventional simulation method, we directly perform full EM analysis of the device to accurately determine its linear response. The extracted S-parameters are then fed into a nonlinear harmonic balance simulator with Josephson junctions modeled as circuit elements. By doing so, the linear and gain properties of the JTWPA are extracted. Different factors that impact device performance including gain compression, phase matching, and fabrication imperfections are further investigated and modeled. A good agreement between simulation and measurements is identified, establishing the effectiveness of our approach in designing quantum parametric amplifiers.

titles.title: Designing Josephson Traveling-Wave Parametric Amplifiers: EM-Circuit Cosimulation and Experimental Validation

abstracts.value: The q-plate is a spatially inhomogeneous SU(2) birefringent optical element that has garnered significant interest due to its ability to mediate the spin-orbit interaction of light and facilitate the generation of structured light with singularities. The q-plate features a spatially varying fast axis orientation defined by three parameters: the topological charge q, retardance delta, and the offset angle $alpha_0$. While the parameter alpha_0 can be changed many times by rotation, any change in the charge and/or retardance entails the fabrication of a new plate. This limitation can be overcome through the concept of an effective waveplate, where multiple waveplates, homogeneous or inhomogeneous, are aligned coaxially so that, under specific constraints, the composite system emulates the behavior of a single effective waveplate. This work presents a comprehensive mathematical formalism for realizing an effective waveplate through a cascaded configuration of three q-plates, each chosen as either a quarter-wave q-plate, a half-wave q-plate, or a combination thereof. Some configurations offer tunability of the retardance over the full range from 0 to $2pi$, even though q-plates with fixed retardances of $pi/2$ and pi are used in sequence to form an effective q-plate. This feature enables holonomic polarization walk on the higher-order Poincare sphere. Such a capability holds significant potential for applications involving structured light associated with the higher-order Poincare sphere, particularly in controlled polarization transformations and polarization-topology engineering.

titles.title: Mathematics of effective q-plate in polarization optics

abstracts.value: Understanding the weak thermal links in supporting legs of transition edge sensors (TES) is crucial for developing highly sensitive bolometers used in cosmic microwave background detection. Conventional current-biased differential resistance measurements under varying temperature (R-T) are commonly used to characterize the resistance (R) and critical temperature (Tc) of TES. However, this method often encounters some phenomena: the bias current will affect the transition temperature obtained during Tb drop testing, as well as the obtained shape of the transition region. This behavior stems from the weak thermal links of TES under current bias, limiting R-T method to providing only rough information about the TES transition regime sometimes. The detailed and accurate performance parameters typically obtained via voltage-biased current-voltage I–V measurements using superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). In fact, the positive electro-thermal feedback induced by current bias contains valuable insights into the device’s intrinsic properties. This work focuses on elaborating the underlying mechanism: by analyzing the current-induced suppression of measured transition temperature in R-T measurements, we extract key parameters including thermal conductance (G), thermal exponent (n), Tc, and saturation power (Psat). This study provides intuitive calculations and visualizations of the electro-thermal behaviors induced by current bias in TES devices and offers a simple and rapid complementary tool for electro-thermal parameter extraction. For batch TES fabrication, it can serve as a pre-screening tool to improve the efficiency of subsequent high-precision SQUID-based I–V characterization.

titles.title: Unraveling Current-Bias-Induced Transition Discrepancy in Transition-Edge Sensors in R-T Tests and Establishing a Reliable Characterizing Method

abstracts.value: When constructing high-field magnets with nonmetallic formers, quench protection of slot-type magnets such as discrete-cosine-theta and canted-cosine-theta becomes particularly challenging, as nonmetallic structures cannot provide the quench-back effect. To address this issue, a 6+1 cable (six superconducting wires and one center cooper wire) configuration has been proposed. During a quench, the central copper strand acts as an internal heater, inducing the quench-back effect. However, the presence of the copper strand reduces the available slot space, thereby limiting the effective engineering current density. To further improve both the current density and protection performance, the coupling-loss induced quench (CLIQ) method has been introduced and applied to seven-strand superconducting cables without a central copper strand. In this study, an electro-thermal coupling model is employed to first validate, through experiment–simulation comparison, the effectiveness of quench-back protection in 6+1 cables. The same model is then extended to analyze and predict the quench protection performance of seven-strand cables under CLIQ. The results demonstrate that CLIQ can effectively trigger uniform quenching, significantly reducing the quench integral and hot-spot temperature, thereby ensuring the reliable protection of the magnet.

titles.title: Electro-Thermal Modeling of Quench-Back and CLIQ Protection for Multistrand Superconducting Magnets

abstracts.value: Superconducting transmon qubits form the backbone of today’s leading quantum processors, where high field dispersive readout relies fundamentally on the shape and temporal structure of microwave control pulses. While transmon qubits offer improved robustness against charge noise, their performance is still strongly influenced by environmental coupling, particularly the Purcell effect and by the spectral characteristics of the readout pulses used for state preparation and logic operations. In this article, we present a rigorous comparative analysis of qubit coherence dynamics using measurement under four relevant configurations: a single-step rectangular pulse without Purcell decay, a single-step pulse subject to Purcell-induced relaxation, a two-step shaped pulse without Purcell effects, and a two-step shaped pulse incorporating Purcell decay. By solving the time-dependent Lindblad master equation for a three-level transmon system, we illustrate how readout pulse shaping and Purcell filtering independently and jointly influence qubit population dynamics, excited-state lifetime, and the final-state fidelity. The results demonstrate that two-step readout pulse shaping significantly improves coherence by suppressing overshoot and reducing higher level population transfer, while the inclusion of Purcell mitigation further stabilizes the dynamics and enhances fidelity. The most notable observation is that the combined application of pulse shaping and Purcell filtering produces the most stable and highest fidelity qubit state discrimination. This unified perspective constitutes the central novelty of this article. Such a comparative framework, integrating pulse engineering with environmental decay modeling, has received limited explicit treatment in prior literature. The findings provide critical insights for optimizing both readout protocols and quantum hardware design in large-scale superconducting quantum systems.

abstracts.value: The circular electron positron collider (CEPC) represents a major international scientific project, with its detector magnet proposing the use of the aluminum-stabilized stacked REBCO tapes cable (ASTC) in its high-temperature superconducting (HTS) design. To ensure the long-term stable and safe operation of this magnet, a thorough investigation on the quench behavior of the ASTC is imperative. This article presents a comprehensive 3-D quench simulation model for the ASTC, incorporating coupled electromagnetic-thermal analysis. The model is employed to simulate the global quench characteristics of the cable under liquid nitrogen immersion cooling, explicitly accounting for internal electrical contact resistance and thermal contact resistance. Key quench parameters, namely, the minimum quench energy (MQE) and quench propagation velocity (QPV), are investigated under varying operational currents, with particular emphasis on performance under adiabatic conditions representing the worst-case scenario. Simulation results demonstrate the significant role of the aluminum stabilizer in current sharing and heat conduction, contributing to the cable's stability and recoverability. The study confirms that the ASTC exhibits robust operational stability, where local quenches are unlikely to propagate into global quench events under effective cooling, thereby validating its suitability for the CEPC detector magnet application. The developed multiphysics model and simulation methodology provide a valuable framework for subsequent quench analysis of superconducting magnets.

titles.title: Study on Quench Behavior of Aluminum-Stabilized Stacked REBCO Tapes Cable

abstracts.value: Topological defects in two-dimensional conformal field theories (CFTs) are canonical examples of generalized symmetries in quantum field theories. They not only encode key features of the underlying theory, but their study has also enhanced our understanding of renormalization group (RG) flows in theories that contain them. Lattice models exist which discretize the states, energy-momentum tensor, and primary fields of many 2D CFTs, raising the natural question of whether topological defects can be similarly discretized. In this thesis, we demonstrate that in many cases all topological defects of minimal model CFTs can be discretized, enabling analytical and ab-initio numerical computations of their properties. In some of these constructions, we make essential use of the integrable structure of the underlying lattice models. The lattice realization of these operators also permits the study of defect RG flows between CFTs with different topological defects inserted. These topological defects and defect RG flows are realized on the lattice not only for Hermitian but also for non-Hermitian lattice Hamiltonians. Studying topological defects in minimal model CFTs on the lattice has also opened the door to a deeper understanding of topological defects in CFTs where they remain poorly understood.

titles.title: Topological defects in conformal field theories and their lattice realizations

abstracts.value: The increasing use of robotic platforms in hazardous and magnetically complex environments, such as underground research facilities at CERN, demands a detailed understanding of how strong external magnetic fields affect electromechanical actuation. Quadruped robots equipped with electromagnetic (EM) motors are particularly vulnerable, as their actuators interact directly with ambient magnetic fluxes, generating additional mechanical forces and moments that can compromise stability, trajectory tracking and overall operational safety. This work presents a modeling framework for estimating the equivalent magnetic moment of an EM motor subjected to high-intensity magnetic fields. The proposed approach combines numerical simulation datasets with an analytical dipole-based formulation to derive a computationally efficient model capable of predicting magnetic-induced mechanical disturbances in real/time. The model accounts for the dependence of the magnetic moment on both the external field intensity and the motor’s orientation relative to the field lines, enabling the control system to anticipate disturbance torques and implement appropriate compensation strategies. The accuracy and reliability of the model were validated experimentally by rotating a Unitree GO-M8010-6 motor within controlled magnetic fields and comparing the measured torques with the model predictions. The results demonstrate close agreement in both trend and amplitude, confirming that the proposed formulation can provide the level of fidelity required for real-time control applications in magnetically harsh environments.

titles.title: Modeling mechanical disturbances induced by high intensity magnetic fields on electric motors

abstracts.value: A central theme of Physical Mathematics is that the partition function of a supersymmetric quantum field theory on a space $X$ often admits multiple interpretations, and the interplay between these viewpoints is a powerful source of new mathematical results. This thesis contributes to this dialogue in three directions, all within the framework of 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetry. In part I, we consider 5d $mathcal{N}=1$ $SU(2)$ super Yang-Mills theory on $X imes S^1$, with $X$ a closed smooth four-manifold. A partial topological twisting along $X$ renders the theory formally independent of the metric on $X$. The theory depends on the spin structure and the circumference $R$ of $S^1$. The coefficients of the $R$-expansion of the partition function are Witten indices, which are identified with $L^2$-indices of Dirac operators on moduli spaces of instantons. The partition function encodes BPS indices for instanton particles on a spatial manifold $X$, and these indices are special cases of K-theoretic Donaldson invariants. When the 't Hooft flux of the gauge theory is nonzero and $X$ is not spin, the 5d theory can be anomalous, but this anomaly can be canceled by coupling to a line bundle with connection for the global $U(1)$ "instanton number symmetry". For $b^+_2(X) > 0$ we derive the partition function from integration over the Coulomb branch of the effective 4d low-energy theory. When $X$ is toric we also use equivariant localization with respect to the $mathbb{C}^* imes mathbb{C}^*$ symmetry. The two methods lead to the same results for the wall-crossing formula. We also determine path integrals for four-manifolds with $b^+_2(X) > 1$. Our results agree with those for algebraic surfaces by Göttsche, Kool, Nakajima, Yoshioka, and Williams, but apply to a larger class of manifolds. When the circumference of the circle is tuned to special values, the path integral is associated with the 5d superconformal $E_1$ theory. Topological invariants in this case involve generalizations of Seiberg-Witten invariants. In part II, we relate the Macdonald index of a 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ SCFT to the Hilbert series of the arc space of the Zhu algebra of the corresponding Schur vertex operator algebra. Using this, we conjecture a simple closed-form formula for the Macdonald index of the $(A_1, D_{2n+1})$ Argyres-Douglas theories. We perform checks of the formula against the known Schur limits and RG flows. To match the Schur limit, we prove new $q$-series identities. Moreover, we propose a refinement of the Kontsevich-Soibelman wall-crossing operator for a class of 4d $mathcal{N}=2$ SCFTs whose Coulomb branch admits a source/sink chamber (a chamber in which the BPS quiver consists of only source and sink nodes) and whose nodes with valency greater than 2 are either all sources or all sinks. We present strong evidence that the trace of this refined operator computes the Macdonald index of the theory. In particular, we conjecture new closed-form expressions for the Macdonald indices of the $(A_1, mathfrak{g})$ Argyres-Douglas theories for any simply-laced Lie algebra $mathfrak{g}$.

titles.title: Two Studies in Physical Mathematics: K-theoretic Donaldson Invariants and Macdonald Indices of Argyres-douglas Theories

abstracts.value: This article presents the design of a four-channel front-end application specific integrated circuit (ASIC), ATLAS liquid argon front-end (ALFE), developed for the readout of the liquid-argon calorimeter (LAr) detector in the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). ALFE enables the readout of current signals induced in the LAr with a dynamic range (DR) exceeding 16 bits, while ensuring seamless operation in a system comprising nearly 200000 channels with detector capacitances ranging from 0.16 to 2 nF per channel. Each analog front-end (AFE) channel provides configurable and matched input impedance of either 50 or $25~\Omega $ , measures an equivalent noise current (ENI) of $\mathbf {47.5}$ or $\mathbf {147.5~\text {nA}}$ , achieves sub- $\mathbf {0.2\% }$ integral non-linearity (INL) for signal peak measurement, and maintains a power supply rejection (PSR) exceeding 14 dB up to $\mathbf {1~\text {MHz}}$ . Each AFE channel incorporates a low-noise amplifier (LNA) with a noise figure (NF) of 0.5 or 0.95 dB and an input-referred voltage noise density of $ \mathbf {0.28~\text {nV}/(\text {Hz})^{1/2} }$ . This LNA is implemented with a fully-differential amplifier (FDA) enclosed in an asymmetric differential feedback (ADF), followed by a two-gain fully differential CR–RC2 bandpass filter (BPF). ALFE can withstand a radiation-induced total ionizing dose (TID) exceeding 1.4 Mrad. Besides the four AFE channels, ALFE integrates an analog trigger-sum (ATS), an SEE/SEU-tolerant I2C interface, voltage and current references, and current digital-to-analog converters (DACs).

titles.title: A 0.5-/0.95-dB NF, 50-/25-$\Omega$ Configurable CMOS Front-End ASIC for the Readout of Liquid Argon Calorimeter in the LHC

abstracts.value: The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the NewAthena X-ray telescope will use a 1504-pixel array of transition-edge sensor (TES) microcalorimeters, read out via time division multiplexing. To allow testing of multiplexer chips before TES integration, each unit cell includes a “TES-bypass” resistor that substitutes for a TES during characterization. After integration, this resistor remains as a high-resistance shunt: minimal for DC operation, but it can influence the frequency response due to its placement with the Nyquist inductor. We modeled the modified bias circuit, derived the small-signal response, and evaluated noise contributions, including Johnson noise from the bypass resistor. We analyzed the effects on pulse height, slew rate, and energy resolution. Simulations were compared with measurements from prototype X-IFU microcalorimeters. Our results indicate that as long as the resistor value exceeds the TES dynamic resistance, performance is largely unaffected.

abstracts.value: In this article, we report the electrical (dark) characterization of lumped-element kinetic inductance detectors (LEKIDs) fabricated from a titanium/aluminum bilayer and designed for broadband absorption in the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$W$</tex-math></inline-formula>-band (75–110 GHz). These detectors are prototypes for future quantum chromodynamics axion search experiments within the Canfranc axion detection experiment (CADEx), which demand sub-<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$10^{-19} \text{W}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> sensitivities under low optical backgrounds. We combine a Mattis–Bardeen analysis to the temperature dependence of the detector parameters with noise spectroscopy to determine the electrical noise equivalent power (NEP). The minimum measured value for the electrical NEP is <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$\sim 3 \times 10^{-19} \text{W}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Across the measured temperature range, we find that quasiparticle lifetime deviates from the expected BCS recombination law. Our analysis suggests that nonequilibrium relaxation is governed by spatial inhomogeneities in the superconducting gap and phonon diffusion effects. This work sets the road-map to achieve suitable and ultra-sensitive detectors in the <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$W$</tex-math></inline-formula>-band for dark matter axion search experiments.

abstracts.value: The BULLKID-DM experiment aims to detect weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP)-like potential dark matter particles with masses below 1 GeV/c<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{2}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Sensing these particles is challenging, as it requires nuclear recoil detectors characterized by high exposure and an energy threshold in the order of 100 eV, achieved with cryogenic phonon detectors. BULLKID-DM introduces a detector that combines the low energy threshold with a new scalable technology, reaching a total target mass of 800 g. The core detector of the BULLKID-DM experiment is composed of 16 100 mm silicon wafers, each segmented in 145 dice for a total of more than 2000 units, each sensed by a microwave kinetic inductance detector (MKID). The MKIDs on each wafer are coupled to a single transmission line and read using a frequency division multiplexing approach by the room-temperature data acquisition. In this contribution, we describe and assess the design of the room-temperature readout electronics system, including the selected hardware components and the field-programmable gate array firmware, which contains the real-time signal processing stages for tone generation, frequency demultiplexing, and event triggering. We evaluate the system on the ZCU216 board, a commercial evaluation card built around a radio-frequency system-on-chip with integrated high-speed digital–analog converters and analog–digital converters, and connected it to a custom-designed analog front-end for signal conditioning.

titles.title: Real-Time Readout System Design for the BULLKID-DM Experiment: Enhancing Dark Matter Search Capabilities

abstracts.value: Microwave superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) multiplexers (µMUX) have become a key technology for the readout of large arrays of low-temperature detectors, particularly in cosmic microwave background experiments. A critical element of this technique is the flux-ramp modulation signal, whose noise, especially at low frequencies, directly limits the readout performance. This work proposes and experimentally demonstrates the use of a Josephson arbitrary waveform synthesizer (JAWS) as a low-noise, high-precision source for generating the sawtooth-shaped flux-ramp signal required in µMUX readout systems. The JAWS, based on the AC Josephson effect, provides intrinsically quantized and spectrally pure waveforms with excellent signal-to-noise ratio. The operation of a 9000-junction JAWS array is characterized and integrated with a cryogenic µMUX device and a custom software defined radio (SDR)-based readout system. With this setup, the noise floor level around the harmonic typically used for phase demodulation of the SQUID signal to recover the detector signal was <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$-104 \,\mathrm{dB}{\mathrm{c}} / \mathrm{Hz}$</tex-math></inline-formula>, and the signal-to-noise ratio of this harmonic was <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$73 \,\mathrm{dB}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using JAWS-based waveform synthesis for µMUX flux-ramp generation.

titles.title: Josephson Arbitrary Waveform Synthesizer for Flux-Ramp Modulation in Microwave SQUID Multiplexers

abstracts.value: This study evaluated the performance of lumped element kinetic inductance detectors (LEKIDs) fabricated on yttria-stabilized zirconia (YSZ) substrates with yttria concentrations of 9.5%, 13%, and 20% . We focus on the application of LEKIDs in the search for undiscovered double-beta decay on <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{94}$</tex-math></inline-formula>Zr and are developing a detector for this purpose. The yttria concentration of YSZ affects its properties, such as ionic conductivity, necessitating analysis of its effects for detector applications. In this work, LEKIDs made with niobium thin films were tested for resonant frequency, quality factor, and temperature-dependent behavior. No significant differences in yttria concentration were observed that would affect LEKID performance. However, temperature-control measurements confirmed a large two-level system contribution, regardless of the yttria concentration.

abstracts.value: In this article, we present the design of a hybridization and integration of three integrated circuits, each cooled to different cryogenic temperatures. abstracts.value: The CCAT Observatory’s primary science instrument, Prime-Cam, is nearing readiness for deployment to the Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope in the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. When fully deployed, Prime-Cam will field approximately 100 000 kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) across seven instrument modules making both broadband and polarimetric measurements. Meanwhile, in-lab characterization of the first CCAT instrument module, a 280-GHz broadband camera fielding over 10 000 KIDs, is currently underway in the test bed instrument Mod-Cam. Both Mod-Cam and Prime-Cam will employ 46-cm-long low-thermal-conductivity flexible circuits (“stripline”) between 4 and 300 K to connect large-format arrays of multiplexed KIDs in each instrument module to readout electronics. The 280-GHz camera currently installed in Mod-Cam uses six of these striplines to read out its over 10 000 detectors. We have examined the thermal and electrical performance of the stripline installed in Mod-Cam in an effort to better optimize the readout chain for deployment in Prime-Cam. We begin by characterizing the oxygen-free high thermal conductivity (OFHC) copper in the stripline traces, allowing for the estimation of thermal loading through these flexible circuits in their configurations in both Mod-Cam and Prime-Cam. We then directly measure the thermal conductivity of the stripline, finding it is best described by <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$kA\,=\,22\pm \text{6}\,T^{0.84\pm 0.09}\,\mathrm{\mu W{\cdot } m{\cdot } K^{-1}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> for temperature ranges of <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$6\,\mathrm{K} < T < 20\,\mathrm{K}$</tex-math></inline-formula> and <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$kA\,=\,0.6\pm \text{0.3}\,T^{-0.4\pm 0.1}\,\mathrm{mW{\cdot } m{\cdot }K^{-1}}$</tex-math></inline-formula> for ranges from <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$20\,\mathrm{K}< T < 80\,\mathrm{K}$</tex-math></inline-formula>. Following our thermal characterizations, we report on the transmission and crosstalk properties of the Mod-Cam readout chain, isolating elevated crosstalk to SMP-SMA transition printed circuit boards that interface with the stripline. This finding validates the stripline circuit as a viable high-density cabling option for large-format array readout.

titles.title: CCAT: Flexible Stripline Circuits for Large-Format Kinetic Inductance Detector (KID) Array Readout

abstracts.value: Kinetic inductance detectors are widely used in millimeter- and submillimeter-wave astronomy, benefiting from their fast response and relative ease of fabrication. The GroundBIRD telescope employs microwave kinetic inductance detectors at 145 and 220 GHz to observe the cosmic microwave background. As a ground-based telescope, it is subject to inherent environmental systematics, namely atmospheric emission and thermal fluctuations of the focal plane temperature. This study models resonance frequency shifts induced by each source using calibrated on-site measurements of precipitable water vapor and temperature. Comparison with observational data confirms the validity of the models and identifies atmospheric loading as the dominant contributor to frequency variation under typical observation conditions.

abstracts.value: Scaling astronomical detectors and quantum devices to larger and larger sizes will require more readout lines. A problem with extra readout lines is the complexity and cost of many coaxial cables in parallel. Furthermore, the thermal loading on the coldest stages via thermal conductivity should be kept at a minimum. Delft circuits provides an eight-channel flexible cabling solution based on stripline technology with Ag or NbTi conductors and polyimide dielectric (flexline) as a solution to these problems. However, a compact and light-tight flex-to-chip interface is lacking, and this would be key to unlocking its full scaling and lightweight potential. Here, we present the design and measurements of a flexline to PCB interface for cryogenic detectors. The flexline is connected securely via a spring-loaded pressing tool, ensuring reliable contact even after thermal contraction. To reduce stray radiation, the chip and connector assembly sits in a light-tight setup. The connector spans a width of 20 mm along one edge of the chip, illustrating the compact design. We show that the flexline connector has an insertion loss of –2 dB at 7 GHz using a probe measurement at room temperature. We also demonstrate the connector with a test chip with kinetic inductance detectors in a dilution refrigerator cooled to 40 mK.

Particle interactions in the sugar were observed with associated scintillation light, indicating a possible channel for particle discrimination.

abstracts.value: Supercritical CO2 (sCO2 ) is of high interest for compact cooling applications, yet local heat transfer data in millimetric scale horizontal tubes under electronics-relevant conditions remain scarce. This work reports local heat transfer coefficients, pressure drops and temperature-inlet-to-outlet values for CO2 at inlet pressures from 7.5 to 8.5 MPa flowing in a 1 mm horizontal stainless-steel tube with 𝐺 = 2130 kg m−2 s −1 ( ̇𝑚 ≈ 1.8 g s−1 ) and uniform Joule heating over 𝐿ℎ = 0.903 m at 𝑞 = 35 kW m−2 . A calorimetric data reduction based on inlet and outlet conditions is combined with an axial enthalpy integration to express results as a function of bulk enthalpy, thus enabling consistent comparison across inlet temperatures. The obtained heat transfer coefficients span from 10 to 60 kW m−2 K −1 and show a systematic dependence on inlet temperature and pressure through the pseudo-critical region. When the fluid near the wall crosses the pseudo-critical point, a first enhancement is observed, associated with the sharp increase in 𝑐𝑝 , causing the collapse of (𝑇𝑤 −𝑇𝑏 ). The overall pressure drop increases steeply as inlet conditions approach the pseudo-critical temperature, whereas the inlet-to-outlet temperature rise decreases and tends to plateau, highlighting the thermal–hydraulic trade-off in this regime. Additionally, comparison with Petukhov (P) and Krasnoshchekov– Kuraeva–Protopopov (KKP) correlations shows that KKP captures about 85% of data within ±20%, while P overpredicts at high heat transfer coefficients due to the lack of consideration of strong radial property variations. These results provide a benchmark dataset of high Reynolds numbers, low heat flux sCO2 heat transfer in 1 mm horizontal channels and show an improved performance of sCO2 as a local single-phase refrigerant, making it a promising alternative for detector and electronics cooling at warm operating temperatures above 31 𝑜C.

titles.title: Effects of inlet temperature and pressure in sCO2 heat transfer in a 1 mm diameter horizontal tube

abstracts.value: LiteBIRD is an experiment dedicated to the measurement of the primordial <inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$B$</tex-math></inline-formula> modes in the cosmic microwave background polarization. This signal is characterized by its faintness, and it is dominated by contamination sources such as galactic foregrounds and instrument systematics. Consequently, the optical system onboard the LiteBIRD satellite must meet several stringent constraints on optical ghosting, and in general, straylight mitigation. The use of microwave absorbing coatings on the 4K-cooled internal surfaces of the telescope enclosure, around the aperture stop and the forebaffle, is required to ensure straylight suppression. Therefore, a selection of materials with suitable optical and thermo-mechanical properties is required. For the LiteBIRD absorbers, a baseline material recipe was selected, based on a mixture of epoxy resins and conductive loading powders. The design features a 3-D textured broadband nonreflective surface, which has been developed to minimize reflections in the 89–448 GHz band. A variation of the design is also under study for the purpose of extending the straylight mitigation toward the lower frequency (40–448 GHz). This will be achieved taking into account the necessary design variations to accommodate the challenging constraints of the mass allocation for the telescope.

titles.title: Optical Characterization of Microwave Absorbers for Straylight Suppression in the LiteBIRD Telescopes

abstracts.value: X-ray microcalorimeter space missions require an anti-coincidence detector to mitigate background events from Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCRs). These high-energy particles mimic an X-ray signal by depositing energy in the microcalorimeter absorber, with the amount proportional to their track length. An anti-coincidence detector, positioned below the main microcalorimeter array, identifies these background events and should respond quickly to a GCR signal, has a low threshold and high dynamic range, and uses a similar readout scheme as the main detector array. For the proposed Line Emission Mapper (LEM) X-ray probe concept, a W and Al-based athermal phonon sensor design, originally developed for the Cryogenic Dark Matter Search, was adapted to cover a large Si substrate (14 cm<inline-formula xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink"><tex-math notation="LaTeX">$^{2}$</tex-math></inline-formula>) with 12 parallel networks of these sensors. This initial prototype for the LEM mission was developed in collaboration with SLAC and Northwestern University, and tested at NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. The prototype demonstrated a combination of low threshold, high dynamic range, and millimeter-scale position discrimination, far exceeding all mission requirements. At the same time, detector modeling efforts were undertaken to understand the rich datasets produced by the prototype. In this work, we expand upon these modeling capabilities to explore new anti-coincidence particle detection designs enabled by the high performance of the LEM prototype. Using G4CMP, an add-on framework to Geant4 for phonon and charge transport in cryogenic detectors, we model the athermal phonon signals generated by GCR events and their collection as quasiparticles in the sensor network. We consider alternative sensor network layouts to maximize GCR event position discrimination, which could reduce false-coincidence events by localizing event rejection in the main array.

titles.title: Simulation Driven Design of a Cryogenic Anti-Coincidence Detector for X-Ray Microcalorimeter Space Missions

abstracts.value: This study investigates the energetic processes, thermodynamic behavior, and quasi-periodic oscillations associated with a quantum-corrected Kerr black hole (BH). A modified space-time geometry is introduced through the parameter β, which incorporates the BH mass M and the non-free parameter α arising from the loop quantum gravity (LQG) framework. The analysis includes determining key static surfaces, such as the event horizon and static limit, and their dependence on the quantum-correction parameter. Examining the Penrose process in this modified geometry shows that quantum corrections modify the efficiency of energy extraction, without imposing a strict bound within the perturbative regime. The efficiency of photons emitted by rotating particles in the ergo-region is found to satisfy ϵ < 0.5, indicating a generally lower energy extraction efficiency compared to the classical Kerr BH. The corresponding deceleration of BH rotation and the response of massive particles involved in the process are analyzed for both classical and quantum-corrected cases. A thermodynamic investigation further reveals the presence of notable phase transitions induced by quantum corrections. Additionally, Keplerian and fundamental oscillatory frequencies are tested, highlighting qualitative differences from the classical Kerr model, and these findings demonstrate that quantum corrections significantly influence the dynamical, thermodynamic, and oscillatory characteristics of rotating BHs.

titles.title: Quantum effects on Penrose energy extraction and black hole thermodynamics

abstracts.value: We propose that early Super Massive Black Holes (SMBHs) grow at an enhanced Eddington rate facilitated by rotation. Recent theoretical work suggests that rotating Black Holes (BHs) can produce winds or jets carrying electric currents. These currents are driven by a pE−2 momentum spectrum of protons and anti-protons, which can reach EeV energies for near-maximal rotation — independent of the BHs mass. This electric current generated in the ergo-region leads to rapid collisions producing anti-particles and lots of pions. The associated electron population suffers extreme losses in the magnetic field observed, so that the protons, anti-protons, neutrons, anti-neutrons and pions altogether, carry a much larger mass/energy per electron than a single proton, while charge is conserved.This factor can be estimated, depends on the spin of the BH, and allows a significant enhancement of Eddington limited accretion. This effect is proposed to explain the rapid growth of early SMBHs observed by James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). The prediction is that these SMBHs rotate rapidly. When compared with cosmological simulations of structure evolution with SMBH formation and evolution without allowing for BH rotation, a second testable prediction is that the gravitational waves produced in ensuing SMBH mergers are enhanced due to high rotation, with ensuing increased total mass.

titles.title: Electric discharges: Early growth of super-massive black holes

abstracts.value: Ce3+–doped gadolinium-based fluoro–oxide (GFO) glass was developed for prospective high-energy physics (HEP) experiment applications. The minimum ionizing particle (MIP) response and timing characteristics of GFO glasses coupled with a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM, 3*3 mm2) were investigated using a cosmic-ray (muon) coincidence setup. The MIP response of a 1 cm-thick glass is 142.1 ± 1.7 p.e., satisfying the criteria for hadron calorimeter applications. As the thickness increases, the MIP responses decrease to 112.7 ± 0.4 (2 cm-thick) and 76.8 ± 1.4 p.e./cm (4 cm-thick). Additionally, Cosmic-ray-induced scintillation shows a dominant slow decay component of ∼500 ns which increases with glass thickness. In this work, appropriately increasing the trigger area remains an effective method to improve the trigger efficiency. According to Monte Carlo simulation, the MIP responses are close to the experimental values, maintaining errors below 6%. The simulated MIP response reaches a maximum value of 361.7 ± 2.7 p.e. for a 5 cm thickness, owing to the short attenuation length of GFO glass which leads to significant photon absorption. Therefore, enhancing its light attenuation length to reduce light loss during internal transmission is currently a critical objective.

abstracts.value: CLLBC is an inorganic detector material of interest for several application spaces, including non-proliferation. The multi-modal aspect of CLLBC, sensitive to gamma-rays, thermal neutrons, and fast neutrons, makes it particularly interesting for Arms Control. To explore the utility of CLLBC for Arms Control, a detector needs to be characterized and optimized to test its performance in relevant scenarios. In addition, validation through simulation is vital for exploring specific use cases for the detector. In this work, a detector with ⌀⌀ 38 mm ×38 mm cylinder CLLBC crystal is used to study pulse shape discrimination of thermal neutrons and gamma-rays, as well as the timing and resolution of the gamma-ray signal for most optimized performance. Additionally, the intrinsic detection efficiency to gamma-rays is characterized through multiple experimental measurements and a high fidelity MCNP model of this detector that was developed and validated against several gamma-ray sources. The characterization of the fast neutrons will be presented in a future article.

titles.title: Characterization and optimization of a CLLBC detector

abstracts.value: We examine the geodesic structure, shadow, quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs), thermodynamic properties, and greybody factors (GBFs) of a static, spherically symmetric black hole (BH) embedded in a beta dark matter halo (DMH). The photon sphere, shadow radius, and photon trajectories grow with increasing DMH density, producing deviations that can be tested against Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) bounds for Sgr A* and M87*. For massive particles, we calculate the innermost stable circular orbit (ISCO), the radiative efficiency, and the epicyclic frequencies, and we read off the epicyclic resonance (ER) model predictions for twin-peak QPOs. With the emcee Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampler, these predictions are compared with observed QPO data from three stellar-mass X-ray binaries (XTE J1550–564, GRO J1655–40, GRS 1915+105), the supermassive BH Sgr A*, and the intermediate-mass candidate M82 X-1, yielding 1σ constraints on the BH mass and the DMH parameter κ for all five sources. The thermodynamic analysis gives a single phase transition whose critical horizon shifts as the halo parameters vary, while the spin-0 GBFs show that the DMH lowers the potential barrier and lets more low-frequency scalar emission through. The beta DMH thus leaves measurable signatures in X-ray timing, shadow imaging, accretion efficiency, and BH ringdown spectra.

titles.title: Astrophysical signatures of black holes in beta dark matter halos: QPO constraints from X-ray binaries, shadow, accretion, and thermal radiation

A B S T R A C T

This study explores the design of sandwich panels using recycled aluminium can rings as the core material. The 
panels are also made with galvanised steel face sheets and a plant-based castor oil adhesive. To assess different 
configurations, two core architectures (cubic and hexagonal) are investigated, and the steel face sheets are tested 
both with and without sanding treatment to increase the roughness of the bonding surfaces. The structural 
properties of the panels are characterised using three-point bending tests, following the ASTM standards C393 
and D7250, as well as the RJS Method (an approach to measure the homogenised flexural modulus of sandwich 
structures). Optimal results are obtained for the hexagonal packing for the core architecture associated with skins 
without sanding: a maximum load of 415 N, representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N⋅m and a mean 
homogenised flexural modulus of 2143 MPa, demonstrating a viable and sustainable method for using 
aluminium cans as a core material for secondary structural applications in the construction and transportation 
industries. Failure analysis reveals that core–skin debonding is the primary cause of structural collapse. This 
indicates that interfacial adhesion is the critical design constraint for these recycled-aluminium sandwich panels.

1. Introduction

Due to increasing global demand for technology and growing climate 
change concerns, engineering and materials science have become 
crucial disciplines for meeting global sustainability challenges and of
fering technologies that balance technical performance, economic 
viability, and environmental responsibility: the three pillars of sustain
ability [1]. The Brundtland Report of 1987 formalised sustainability as 
"development that meets the needs of the present without compromising 
the ability of future generations to meet their own needs." A project is 
considered sustainable if it addresses the three dimensions of sustain
ability: environmental, social, and economic. This requires the model to 
be environmentally responsible, economically viable, and socially rele
vant, serving the interests of both society and the productive sector [2].

To meet sustainability goals, industries like the automotive, naval, 
aeronautical, and aerospace sectors are seeking to develop technologies 
that use lightweight, efficient, and low-cost structures. These charac
teristics are found in sandwich panels, which are used in structural ap
plications ranging from secondary to high-performance [3,4]. Sandwich 
panels represent a significant advance in engineering and materials 
science because they offer a unique combination of low density and high 
stiffness. This is achieved by combining two thin, rigid outer layers (face 
sheets) with a lightweight, thicker core [5].

The increasing demand for sustainable engineering solutions drives 
the development of sandwich panels featuring cores derived from 
recyclable or renewable materials [6,7]. Recent investigations demon
strate promising structural configurations using industrial and urban 
waste, including bottle caps, bamboo rings, and natural fibres [8–11].

Unlike conventional configurations, the discrete nature of the cylindri
cal rings promotes localised instability and progressive collapse in a 
more controlled and distributed manner, thereby enhancing energy 
dissipation. This behaviour remains consistent with instability-driven 
mechanisms reported for thin-walled tubular structures, while high
lighting the additional design flexibility provided by segmented 
geometries.

Additionally, alternative geometries have been explored [8], 
including tubular honeycomb (TH) cells, one of the most recently 
developed core topologies. THs have been used in various applications, 
from supporting oil transportation infrastructure to energy absorption 
panels [12]. Research by Oruganti and Goshi [13] demonstrated that the 
geometric constraints of these cylindrical structures provide them with 
intrinsic stiffness and increased strength.

More broadly, thin-walled cylindrical structures serve as efficient 
energy-absorbing systems due to their progressive collapse mechanisms 
and favourable strength-to-weight ratios. For instance, nested multi- 
tube configurations exhibit significant capacity for energy absorption 
under quasi-static loading, which highlights the mechanical efficiency of 
thin-walled cylindrical architectures [14]. Similarly, investigations into 
recycled beverage cans demonstrate that thin-walled tubular elements 
exhibit promising crashworthiness and energy absorption behaviour, 
reinforcing their potential application in sustainable structural systems 
[15].

This work presents an innovative approach by reusing abundant 
waste aluminium cans as a honeycomb tubular core material, thereby 
avoiding the energy consumption and emissions associated with tradi
tional recycling. These cores are easily created by cutting the cans into 
rings. The sandwich panels comprise galvanised steel face sheets and a 
core of reused aluminium can rings, bonded with a bio-based castor oil- 
derived polyurethane adhesive. These rings are arranged in both cubic 
and hexagonal packing configurations to form the core structure. These 
panels are intended for lightweight structural applications where the 
stiffness-to-weight ratio and energy absorption are critical. Potential 
applications include aerospace and aviation secondary structures (e.g., 
interior partitions), architectural systems (e.g., mezzanine flooring), 
marine structures (e.g., bulkheads), and transportation systems (e.g., 
ramps and tailgates for rail vehicles). Furthermore, the design shows 
potential for high-performance furniture and cabinetry.

The mechanical properties of these panels are evaluated using a 
three-point bending test, following the RJS1 Method [16] and the ASTM 
standards C393 and D7250 [17,18]. This analysis assesses the structural 
feasibility and load-bearing capacity of these sustainable secondary so
lutions for applications in the construction and transportation 
industries.

2. Methodology

2.1. Materials

The sandwich panel consists of 0.53 mm-thick galvanised steel skins 
and a tubular honeycomb core made from reused aluminium rings. The 
rings, each with a thickness of 0.14 mm and a height of 15 mm, are 
arranged in either a hexagonal (Fig. 1a) or cubic (Fig. 1b) packing shape. 
A 1.5 mm thick biobased castor-oil adhesive is used to bond the skins to 
the core, as properly addressed further in the text.

2.2. Characterisation and manufacture

A tensile test is performed on the galvanised steel and aluminium 
sheets in the circumferential direction, following ASTM E8 [19], to 
obtain the elastic modulus, ultimate strength, and ultimate strain. The 

tests are conducted using an Instron testing machine equipped with a 50 
kN load cell, at crosshead speeds of 6 mm/min (galvanised steel) and 0.5 
mm/min (aluminium). A mechanical extensometer is employed for 
strain measurement (Fig. 2). The mechanical properties of the castor-oil 
adhesive were sourced from previous research [20].

The bulk densities of the materials were determined as 2.61 ± 0.23 
g/cm³ for aluminium and 0.98 ± 0.11 g/cm³ for the castor-oil polymer, 
based on the experimental research reported in [20]. The mean bulk 
density of galvanised steel (8.03±0.05 g/cm³) is obtained by the ratio of 
mass and volume measured using a precision scale (accurate to 0.01 g) 
and digital calliper (accurate to 0.01 mm).

The sandwich panels are manufactured through a multi-step process 
designed, as depicited in Fig. 3, to ensure proper assembly and curing. 
First, galvanised steel sheets (185 × 415 mm²) are cut to size according 
to ASTM C393 [17], which specifies a minimum length of two times the 
width and a minimum width of three core cells. To prevent slippage 
during bending tests, an additional safety margin is included. The sur
faces are degreased with detergent and rinsed to remove contaminants. 
Next, the aluminium rings are cut using a Makita® marble saw to ensure 
uniform and precise dimensions. A subset of the galvanised steel sheets 
is sanded on both sides with 100-grit sandpaper to evaluate the effect of 
surface treatment, followed by the same degreasing and washing. The 
assembly process begins by placing the steel skins into a polystyrene 
plate mould covered with a film to prevent resin leakage. The adhesive

3. Results and discussion

3.1. Properties of panel components

Table 2 presents the mean properties of the sandwich panel com
ponents. The mechanical properties values reported for the biobased 
adhesive were obtained from Ref. [20], which investigated similar ma
terials and components to those employed in the present study. The 
tensile modulus of the reused aluminium core is approximately 22% of 
the modulus of elasticity of galvanised steel. Furthermore, the adhesive's 
deformation capacity is 28 times greater than that of the core material. 
These characteristics highlight the complementary roles of the materials 
for a sandwich structure design: rigid skins combined with a less rigid 
but lightweight core structure, with an adhesive layer more ductile than 
the core, which allows for greater deformability.

3.2. Al-tubular core panels: three-point bending properties

Table 3 presents the mean values and standard deviations for the 
following response variables: equivalent density, maximum load, 
experimental flexural modulus, core shear modulus, and modulus of 
toughness. For each property, the best-performing values are under
lined, while the second-best values are in italics. The equivalent density 
of the panels is defined as the ratio between mass and homogenised 
volume. The low variability in equivalent density across all tested con
ditions and replicates, evidenced by minimal standard deviations, 
demonstrates a robust raw materials preparation and manufacturing 
process. Condition C4 demonstrates superior performance across 
approximately 80% of the properties analysed. The only exception is the 
modulus of toughness, for which the highest values are consistently 
observed in configurations with cubic packing, particularly in condition 
C1.

Fig. 5 displays typical force-displacement and mean stress-strain 
curves for each experimental condition, as obtained using the homog
enisation concept from the RJS method [16,24,25]. Condition C4, which 
consists of a hexagonal core with untreated skins, exhibited the highest 
maximum force (~ 415 N), corresponding to an ultimate mean stress of 
approximately 4.25 MPa and a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N⋅m. 
This behaviour suggests that the larger contact area and inherently more 
stable geometry of the hexagonal cell promoted a more uniform load 
distribution, thus increasing the material's resistance, as previously 
discussed. The next highest values are observed in the hexagonal 
configuration with sanded skins (~340 N / ~3.6 MPa), followed by the 
cubic core with sanded skins (~325 N / ~3.4 MPa), and the cubic 
configuration with unsanded skins (~320 N / ~3.3 MPa).

The post-failure load-carrying capacity observed for the cubic 
configuration with skin treatment (blue curve in Fig. 5) indicates the 
activation of specific deformation mechanisms within the tubular core. 
As the load is applied approximately at the panel centre, directly coin
ciding with the core cells, initial failure does not lead to immediate 
structural collapse. Rather, the progressive deformation of the rings 
suggests local rearrangement and partial densification of the cellular 
structure, which enables sustaining additional load following the initial 
peak.

3.3. Al-tubular core panels: statistical analysis of properties

Table 4 summarises the statistical analysis conducted using Design of 
Experiment (DoE) and Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) tools in Minitab 
software. The R2 values (>74%) confirm that the statistical model has a 
satisfactory fit to the experimental data. Additionally, the P-valueAD 

(Anderson-Darling test) and P-valueB (Bartlett test) are presented; values 
greater than 0.05 for both tests indicate data normality and homoge
neity, respectively. These conditions validate the use of ANOVA.

The variables P-valueT, P-valueP, and P-valueTP indicate the signifi
cance of the factors: face treatment, core packing, and the interaction 
between these two factors. A P-value ≤0.05 (in bold, Table 4) suggests 
that the factor or interaction has a statistically significant effect on the 
response variable. P-values (Table 4, highlighted in bold) shall be 
visualised and evaluated using the effect plots presented in Fig. 6. Spe
cifically, when an interaction effect is determined to be statistically 
significant, the separate interpretation of the main effects is typically not 
performed.

The core packing factor significantly affects all properties except 
equivalent density, meaning density does not differ between conditions. 
It's also important to note that the maximum load and flexural strength 
are the only properties influenced by the face treatment. This is likely 
because the treatment enhances the interaction and contact area be
tween the adhesive and the facesheets, which in turn improves the 

panel's performance during plastic deformation. Additionally, the 
interaction between these two factors significantly impacts all the 
modulus properties. The main effect plots and their interactions for each 
response variable, where significant, are shown in Fig. 6(a-e).

The main effect plots for the maximum load are presented in Fig. 6a. 
Skin treatment negatively impacts the maximum load, resulting in an 
8.7% reduction (from ~351 N to ~323 N). Conversely, adopting a 
hexagonal core packing significantly improved the maximum load by 
7.4% (from ~323 N to ~347 N) over the cubic configuration. As 
depicted in Fig. 6b, a comparable effect is evidenced for the flexural 
strength. The optimal performance, with the highest flexural strength, is 
obtained from panels combining untreated skins with the hexagonal 
core. This enhancement is attributed to the hexagonal geometry pro
moting closer packing and reduced gaps between core caps, thereby 
strengthening cell interaction and facilitating a more uniform distribu
tion of internal stresses.

The interaction effect concerning the flexural modulus is delineated 
in Fig. 6c. A statistically significant increase in the flexural modulus 
(approximately 1950 MPa) is attained when utilising hexagonal packing 
compared with the cubic packing (≈1200 MPa). This enhanced perfor
mance is consistent with the advantages of the hexagonal configuration 
in promoting superior volumetric packing and structural integrity.

3.4. Al-tubular core panels: modes of failure

Fig. 7(a–d) illustrates the behaviour of the sandwich panels during 
the three-point bending test for the four conditions proposed in the study 
(C1–C4). The skins of the panels remain intact, even under maximum 
tensile and compressive loads. However, detachment of the lower skin is 
observed in all sandwich panels. Although the panels' construction is 
symmetrical, the manual manufacturing process and its possible varia
tions occasionally result in an unbalanced deflection curvature. This 
behaviour can also generate a heterogeneous stress distribution, over
loading certain regions and consequently causing detachment of the 
adhesive interface outside the beam's central region.

Some samples from conditions C3 and C4 exhibit not only the 
detachment of the lower skin but also a longitudinal rupture of the core 
cells in the out-of-plane direction (see Figs. 7c’–d’). It is noteworthy that 
these conditions withstand the highest bending loads. It is believed that 
the core crack is caused by tensile stresses at the interface with the 
bottom face, which promotes the emergence and propagation of the 
crack. Indirect compressive forces generated in the out-of-plane direc
tion may further contribute to the crack propagation and the opening of 
the tear.

In addition to the core crack, some samples demonstrate a 'counter- 
curvature,' as illustrated in Fig. 7c. This behaviour is attributed to the 
buckling of the upper face, which causes the structure to rotate. This 
rotation subsequently leads to the detachment of the core's lower face. 
Note the lifting of the rings, which indicates an out-of-plane force 
generated by the structure's rotation during the imbalance caused by the 
upper face's buckling.

From a structural perspective, these observations align with the non- 
classical response characteristic of a segmented, friction-dominated core 
system. The discrete ring-based topology, exacerbated by the absence of 
chemical bonding between core elements, results in a lack of transverse 
shear continuity. Consequently, load transfer is governed by localised 
contacts and frictional interactions rather than a continuous stress field, 
which induces stress concentrations and non-uniform deformation pat
terns. This mechanical state inherently suppresses classical failure 

modes, such as core crushing or face wrinkling, favouring instead 
interfacial instability, progressive loss of contact, and localised collapse 
mechanisms.

The experimental results demonstrate that the failure of the pro
posed sandwich panels is governed by interfacial core–skin debonding, 
rather than core crushing or face-sheet yielding. Although the tubular 
core exhibited sufficient compressive stability and the skins remained 
predominantly within the elastic-plastic regime, separation initiated at 
the interface and propagated rapidly under flexural loading. This failure 
mode indicates that the adhesion between the tubular aluminium core 
and the face sheets constitutes the primary structural constraint for the 
current configuration. Consequently, from a design perspective, 
enhancing the bonding strategy, through optimised adhesive selection, 
surface functionalisation, or mechanical interlocking, is a critical pri
ority for increasing the load-bearing capacity of these recycled- 
aluminium sandwich structures.

In this context, applying the RJS homogenisation method, which 
assumes the core makes a negligible contribution to the global flexural 
stiffness, provides a reasonable approximation for the current configu
ration. Although the core comprises metallic tubular elements, the 
experimental response indicates that deformation is predominantly 
shear-dominated, with failure occurring at the core–skin interface rather 
than through core crushing. Consistent with findings in [16], a thickness 
of 1.5 mm yielded the most favourable results. This thickness enhances 
in-plane interlocking between adjacent rings, thereby restricting relative 
movement and increasing the in-plane shear resistance of the core as
sembly. However, its influence on the out-of-plane structural response 
remains limited. This aligns with the observed failure mode, which was 
governed by core–skin debonding, indicating that structural failure was 
driven by out-of-plane separation rather than in-plane shear of the 
tubular lattice.

4. Conclusions

This study investigated the mechanical performance of Al-arched- 
core sandwich panels (support span: 370 mm, width: 185 mm) under

three-point bending. The panels achieved a maximum load of up to 415 
N representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N.m. The measured 
experimental flexural modulus averages 2163 MPa, noting that the 
theoretical flexural modulus under pure bending is projected to reach 35 
GPa under large spans. The hexagonal core packing significantly en
hances the panel's overall flexural strength and stiffness. Conversely, the 
cubic core configuration yields the highest modulus of toughness under 
both skin conditions. This superior toughness stems from the cubic 
packing's enhanced energy absorption capacity prior to fracture, likely 
due to a more gradual redistribution of internal stresses and a less abrupt 
failure mechanism. This suggests the cubic configuration is the more 
advantageous choice for applications demanding toughness (e.g., 
impact or dynamic loading), even with a potential reduction in struc
tural stiffness. The primary failure mechanism across all panels is 
detachment at the core-skin interface, with subsequent failure modes 
including ring rupture and upper face buckling in specific cases. Sta
tistical analysis confirms significant interaction effects between design 
factors, demonstrating that mechanical performance is dictated not by a 
single parameter but by the integrated set of geometric, material, and 
procedural specifications. This necessitates a systemic approach for the 
development of these sandwich structures. In summary, sandwich 
panels fabricated from a core of reused aluminium rings, biobased ad
hesive, and galvanised steel skins represent a promising, sustainable 
alternative that satisfies industrial demands for lightness, strength, and 
environmental responsibility.

The results demonstrate that the structural performance of the 
developed sandwich panels is limited neither by core compressive 
strength nor face-sheet yielding; rather, it is governed by interfacial 
core–skin debonding, which consistently dictated the failure process. 
This finding identifies the core–skin interface as the critical design 
parameter for the future optimisation of sandwich panels fabricated 
with upcycled aluminium-can tubular cores. Consequently, enhancing 
interfacial bond integrity is expected to yield a significant increase in the 
structural efficiency and load-bearing capacity of the proposed 
architecture.

abstracts.value: This study explores the design of sandwich panels using recycled aluminium can rings as the core material. The panels are also made with galvanised steel face sheets and a plant-based castor oil adhesive. To assess different configurations, two core architectures (cubic and hexagonal) are investigated, and the steel face sheets are tested both with and without sanding treatment to increase the roughness of the bonding surfaces. The structural properties of the panels are characterised using three-point bending tests, following the ASTM standards C393 and D7250, as well as the RJS Method (an approach to measure the homogenised flexural modulus of sandwich structures). Optimal results are obtained for the hexagonal packing for the core architecture associated with skins without sanding: a maximum load of 415 N, representing a maximum bending moment of 38.4 N·m and a mean homogenised flexural modulus of 2143 MPa, demonstrating a viable and sustainable method for using aluminium cans as a core material for secondary structural applications in the construction and transportation industries. Failure analysis reveals that core–skin debonding is the primary cause of structural collapse. This indicates that interfacial adhesion is the critical design constraint for these recycled-aluminium sandwich panels.

titles.title: Sustainable sandwich panels from upcycled aluminium cans, galvanised steel, and biobased adhesive
